question: In 2023, the Commission presented a proposal for a Regulation on the welfare of dogs and cats and their traceability.

Subsequently, the European Parliament adopted a firmer stance, stating that euthanasia in shelters must not be allowed as a population management solution and that euthanasia must be limited to cases where recovery is not possible and the animal is experiencing severe pain or suffering that cannot be alleviated.

However, in some Member States the term ‘euthanasia’ is still misused to include the killing of cats and dogs for reasons such as lack of space, cost, administrative inefficiency or to generally make things easier for the competent authorities or structures. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it explicitly support the inclusion, in the final text of the regulation, of a ban on the euthanasia of cats and dogs for reasons of population management, lack of places in shelters, cost or administrative inefficiency, as well as a provision explicitly stipulating that euthanasia must be allowed only in exceptional cases of proven untreatable, irreversible and severe pain or suffering that cannot be alleviated?

Does it intend to support EU-wide binding minimum guarantees, such as an expert opinion from a veterinarian, keeping a complete record of each case as well as a relevant register, and having effective control and penalty mechanisms?

Does it consider that a Member State which allows the actual killing of dogs or cats for the above reasons complies with the objective of ensuring a high level of protection of animal welfare as set out in EU law?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) The co-legislators reached the provisional final political agreement on the Commission proposal for a Regulation on the welfare of dogs and cats and their traceability1 on 25 November 2025, hence negotiations are closed, and new elements are no longer under consideration.

The agreement2 reached between co-legislators defines ‘euthanasia’3 based on the method used to end the life of a dog or cat and the outcome it brings on the animal. It requires that euthanasia is applied when the welfare of a dog or a cat is compromised and the animal experiences severe pain or suffering while its recovery is not achievable.

The agreement does not limit the use of euthanasia exclusively to these specific circumstances. Where these circumstances outlined in point 1 arise, the agreement requires that a veterinarian be consulted to decide whether the dog or cat is to be euthanised to end its suffering. No record or register keeping is foreseen by the veterinarian.

Member States are required to lay down rules on penalties applicable to infringements of the upcoming Regulation. Other Union legislation4 requires Member States to conduct official controls for the verification of compliance with the new rules. Those obligations also concern the issue of euthanasia. The Commission helps develop and adopt international animal health and welfare standards through the WOAH5.

WOAH standards6 require dog population management programmes to be based on a national context and tailored to local circumstances. They further specify that euthanasia alone is ineffective for long-term population control and, if used, must comply with WOAH killing standards and be implemented in combination with other measures to achieve effective long-term population management.

12/1334329EN.pdf. 3 Euthanasia means the act of inducing death using a method that causes a rapid and irreversible loss of consciousness with a minimum of pain and distress, ending the life of the dog or cat.

4 Regulation (EU) 2017/625 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 15 March 2017 on official controls and other official activities performed to ensure the application of food and feed law, rules on animal health and welfare, plant health and plant protection products (Official Controls Regulation), OJ L 95, 7.4.2017, pp. 1. http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/625/oj. 5 World Organisation for Animal Health.

6 Terrestrial Animal Health Code, Section 7, Animal Welfare, Chapter 7.7., Dog population management, https://www.woah.org/en/what-we-do/standards/codes-andmanuals/#chapter/?rid=82&volume_no=1&ismanual=false&language=102&standard_type=5&animal_type=7.
